summary.text: The first law of thermodynamics is the law of conservation of energy applied to heat and work: energy cannot be created or destroyed, only changed from one form to another.
A system's internal energy changes with the heat and work moving into or out of it, and in an isolated system the sum of all energy stays constant.
It also means a machine that produces work with no energy supplied, a perpetual motion machine of the first kind, is impossible.

facts.label: Path dependence
facts.value: Heat and work depend on the path; internal energy change does not

facts.label: Full statements
facts.value: Given in 1850 by Clausius and Rankine

facts.label: Mayer's friction test
facts.value: In 1842 he measured a temperature rise in paper pulp

items.prompt: A paddle churns water in an insulated tub and the water warms. What did Joule's version of this experiment pin down?

options.label: The motion creates new energy from nothing
Water has a fixed temperature it must reach
A set amount of mechanical work gives a unit of heat
Friction destroys energy as the paddle slows

items.explain: Joule measured how much mechanical work was needed to produce a unit of heat, using paddle rotation in a vat of water among other methods.

items.prompt: Inside a sealed, insulated box a lamp turns electrical energy into light and heat. How does the total energy of everything in the box change?

options.label: It stays the same, only its forms change
It drops, because the light is lost
It rises, because the lamp makes more energy
It cancels out and reaches zero

items.explain: In an externally isolated system, even with internal changes, the sum of all forms of energy is constant.

items.prompt: Two engines raise the internal energy of their gas by exactly the same amount, one mostly with heat and the other mostly with work. Is that possible?

options.label: No, since the heat and work must match exactly
Yes, since different mixes can give the same change
No, since work always changes internal energy more
Yes, but only if the gas is also lost

items.explain: A given change in internal energy can be achieved by different combinations of heat and work.

items.prompt: A gas is heated and compressed. Afterward, which quantity describes the gas itself rather than how it got there?

options.label: The heat that was added
The work that was done on it
The route taken during the process
Its internal energy

items.explain: Internal energy is a property of the system, while heat and work describe the process.

items.prompt: A system does work on its surroundings with no heat or work supplied from outside. Where does that energy come from?

options.label: It is created fresh out of nothing
Its own internal energy, which is consumed
The work itself, which costs nothing
The empty space around the system

items.explain: Work done by a system requires that its internal energy be consumed, and the loss must be resupplied by outside heat or work.

items.prompt: You squeeze a gas in a cylinder while the cylinder sits on a hot plate. Which two kinds of energy transfer are at play?

options.label: Work and heat
Heat and entropy
Work and temperature
Pressure and volume

items.explain: For a process without transfer of matter, the first law distinguishes two principal forms of energy transfer: heat and thermodynamic work.

paragraphs.heading: Energy is never lost
paragraphs.text: The first law of thermodynamics is the conservation of energy, written for thermodynamic processes. Energy can change from one form into another, but it can never be made or destroyed. So in a system cut off from everything outside, the total of all its forms of energy stays the same, even as things change inside it.

paragraphs.heading: Heat, work and internal energy
paragraphs.text: When no matter flows in or out, energy can cross into or out of a system in two main ways: as heat or as work. The law also defines internal energy, a running total that keeps track of how heat, work and matter moving in and out change a system. For a closed system, the rise in internal energy equals the heat the system takes in minus the work it does.

paragraphs.heading: State versus path
paragraphs.text: Internal energy belongs to the system itself, while heat and work describe a process, not the system. That means the same change in internal energy can come from different mixes of heat and work. Heat and work depend on the route a process takes. The change in internal energy depends only on where the system starts and where it ends up.

paragraphs.heading: No free work
paragraphs.text: Another way to state the law is that a perpetual motion machine of the first kind cannot exist. When a system does work on its surroundings, it uses up some of its internal energy. To keep working, it must have that energy put back, either as heat from an outside source or as work from an outside machine.

paragraphs.heading: Finding the law
paragraphs.text: Early ideas about heat had to contend with rival views such as the caloric theory. Between 1842 and 1845 James Prescott Joule measured the mechanical equivalent of heat. His 1845 paper gave a number for the work needed to make one unit of heat, based on heat from friction in a resistor carrying electricity and from a paddle turning in a tub of water. Rudolf Clausius and William Rankine each gave a complete statement of the law in 1850.

paragraphs.heading: A slippery quantity
paragraphs.text: Because it is defined through changes, internal energy has no single fixed value. It is set only up to an added constant, which can be chosen to put the zero wherever is convenient. In practice, internal energy is usually given relative to a standard reference state picked by agreement.
